title: Peripersonal Space: Humans’ Got Talent
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter (Josh's recent septoplasty and stints removed), then explore peripersonal space (PPS), the zone around the body within arm's reach, and how it relates to body schema, personal space, and proxemics. They cover early neurology (Henry Head, Gordon Holmes, W. R. Brain), Heinie Hediger's animal flight distance work, Giacomo Rizzolatti's macaque neuron studies, Michael Graziano's electrical stimulation experiments, the 1997 book The Space Around Us, how tools (rakes, sticks, screwdrivers, cars) extend PPS, stroke and laser-pointer studies, factors that change PPS (pregnancy, status, claustrophobia, culture, limb immobilization), Edward Hall's proxemics and cultural comfort distances, and mirror neurons. A listener mail segment about rejected vanity license plates and a plug for Peacock shows close the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh describes his recent septoplasty and stint removal, and Chuck says he's glad Josh picked the peripersonal space topic. They preview body schema and the idea that the space within arm's reach shapes how we interact with the world.

segments.title: Body schema and early neurology
segments.summary: The hosts define body schema and note that even fruit flies have a version of it. They describe early neurologists Henry Head and Gordon Holmes, who studied brain damage and body position, and W. R. Brain, who described grasping and walking distance spaces. They discuss the hat example showing the brain factors in worn objects.

segments.title: Defense origins and exaptation
segments.summary: Philosophers Carmen Kline and Frederique de Vignemont are cited as proposing that peripersonal space evolved from self-defense. The hosts relate this to keeping objects within grasping reach and call it an exaptation.

segments.title: Heinie Hediger and animal flight distance
segments.summary: Swiss zoo director Heinie Hediger studied flight distance, defense distance and critical distance in animals, defining a tame animal as one with zero flight distance. His work later influenced proxemics.

segments.title: Macaque neuron studies: Rizzolatti and Graziano
segments.summary: Giacomo Rizzolatti found neurons in macaques that fired to touch or nearby visual stimuli within peripersonal space. Michael Graziano used electrical stimulation to make monkeys flinch defensively, and blocking those neurons removed the flinch.

segments.title: The Space Around Us and location-specific neurons
segments.summary: Rizzolatti and colleagues' 1997 book The Space Around Us argued neurons respond to location rather than stimulus type. Andreas Arena found PPS size varies by body part and changes shape as body parts approach each other. Bufacchi and Iannetti showed PPS is graded and depends on object motion.

segments.title: Tools extend peripersonal space
segments.summary: The hosts describe how using tools like sticks, screwdrivers, rakes and cars extends the brain's peripersonal space. Anna Berti and Francesca Frassinetti's stroke patient study compared finger, laser pointer and stick. A Japanese monkey rake study showed the space extends only when the rake is used as a tool. Driving and Chuck's Australia driving anecdote are discussed.

segments.title: Shared space, factors that change PPS, and claustrophobia
segments.summary: The hosts discuss shared peripersonal space when objects like batons are passed, and factors that change PPS: anxiety, culture, spinal injury, immobilization, pregnancy, social status, and claustrophobia. They mention Chattanooga attractions Rock City and Ruby Falls as tight-space examples.

segments.title: Proxemics, Edward Hall, and cultural comfort distances
segments.summary: Proxemics, named by anthropologist Edward Hall, is described along with the intimate, personal, social and public distance zones. The hosts discuss how American comfort distances compare to other cultures and how city layouts may reflect personal space norms.

segments.title: Personal space vs peripersonal space and paracutaneous space
segments.summary: Josh offers his view that personal space is an evolved defensive zone while peripersonal space is an extension that allows interaction with the environment. They mention paracutaneous space, the thin zone near the skin, and a philosophical essay on boundaries.

segments.title: Mirror neurons and monkeys watching grasping
segments.summary: The hosts summarize mirror neurons, which fire when watching others act. A study showed monkeys' mirror neurons responded more when a person was closer to an apple, and a clear barrier reduced firing.

segments.title: Closing banter
segments.summary: The hosts joke about whispering and personal space, and wrap the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: rejected vanity license plates
segments.summary: A listener named Elijah from Utah writes about lists of rejected vanity license plates. The hosts discuss the plate lists and plug the Peacock show Friend of the Family and Andy Sierra's show The Resort.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and invite listener email.
